original_question: In the setting of Theorem 5.1, let C be a class of infinite sequences of abelian groups, closed under isomorphism, such that there exist finitely presented groups G_1 and G_2 with the same first homology H_1(G_1) isomorphic to H_1(G_2), with H_*(G_1) in C and H_*(G_2) not in C. Theorem 5.1 proves that the set of finite presentations P for which the integral homology sequence H_*(P) belongs to C is not recursive. Under what additional hypotheses on C can this conclusion be strengthened by replacing 'not recursive' with 'not recursively enumerable'?
target_in_paper: Question 5.2 in Section 5, immediately following Theorem 5.1.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the relevant setup from Theorem 5.1: an isomorphism-closed class C of infinite sequences of abelian groups, the existence of finitely presented groups G1 and G2 with the same first homology but opposite membership in C, and the conclusion that the set of finite presentations P with H_*(P) in C is not recursive. It also correctly targets the paper's next natural question, namely whether this can be strengthened from nonrecursive to non-recursively-enumerable. That is exactly the issue raised in Question 5.2.
missing_details: The paper's official target is not a new theorem but the open problem stated as Question 5.2 immediately after Theorem 5.1.
The notation H_*(G) must be defined explicitly as the infinite sequence (H_1(G), H_2(G), H_3(G), ...) of integral homology groups.
It should be stated that all homology groups are taken with integer coefficients.
The phrase "closed under isomorphism" should be made explicit: two sequences (A_1, A_2, ...) and (A'_1, A'_2, ...) are considered isomorphic when A_i isomorphic to A'_i for every i.

The decision problem concerns the set of all finite presentations P, not directly the set of isomorphism classes of finitely presented groups; one should say that H_*(P) means the homology sequence of the group presented by P.

Remark 5.3 should be acknowledged: if C does not satisfy the hypothesis of Theorem 5.1, then membership of H_*(P) in C depends only on H_1(P), so the interesting strengthening problem is really for classes C that do satisfy the theorem's hypothesis.
The official wording in the paper is broader and sharper than "under what additional hypotheses on C": it asks for a characterization of when one may replace "recursive" by "recursively enumerable."
refined_question: Let C be a class of infinite sequences (A_1, A_2, A_3, ...) of abelian groups, closed under componentwise isomorphism, and for a finitely presented group G let H_*(G) := (H_1(G), H_2(G), H_3(G), ...) denote its integral homology sequence. Assume there exist finitely presented groups G_1 and G_2 such that H_1(G_1) isomorphic to H_1(G_2), H_*(G_1) belongs to C, and H_*(G_2) does not belong to C. Theorem 5.1 shows that the set of finite presentations P for which H_*(P) belongs to C is not recursive. For which such classes C can this conclusion be strengthened to say that the set of finite presentations P with H_*(P) in C is not recursively enumerable?
equivalent_formulation: Question 5.2: When can one replace "recursive" by "recursively enumerable"?
justification: The draft is already very close to the paper's actual intent, but the nearest official formulation is the open problem stated as Question 5.2 in Section 5, not a restatement of Theorem 5.1. Section 5 introduces the notation H_*(G) for the full integral homology sequence, states Theorem 5.1, and then immediately asks when its conclusion can be sharpened from nonrecursive to non-recursively-enumerable. Remark 5.3 adds an important hidden scope condition: if C fails the hypothesis of Theorem 5.1, then the problem collapses to one about the first homology group alone. So a stand-alone, paper-faithful version should include the theorem's hypothesis, the definition of H_*(G), the meaning of isomorphism of sequences, and the fact that recursion-theoretic adjectives apply to the set of finite presentations.
